pulls.title: util: Add and use AssertUnreachable
pulls.body:
The current code uses assertions with falsy literal values in a few places. This is perfectly fine, but this comes with a bit of confusion sometimes:

* `assert(false)` may cause confusion when it is unclear if `NDEBUG` can disable it. (The intention is to disallow `NDEBUG` compilation). Also, it can lead to warnings when used with clang-cl.exe (GCC seems to understand it)
* `Assert(false)` hides the noreturn attribute behind a function call, which may cause GCC return-type warnings. (Clang seems to understand it)

See https://godbolt.org/z/h7PT3jh3Y for the clang-cl/GCC warning reproducer.

* When C++23 will be allowed, devs may prefer `std::unreachable`. However, this is unsafe and will invoke UB.
* There is confusion why a `CHECK_NONFATAL` macro exists, but no fatal equivalent.

Fix all those issues by:

* Adding a new `AssertUnreachable`, which directly calls the noreturn `assertion_fail` helper.
* Adding an `assert_falsy` linter to enforce code to use this macro.

pulls.title: rpc: Return the right RPCErrorCode more consistently
pulls.body:
Currently, rpc code may return the wrong `RPCErrorCode`. This is perfectly fine, because they should be hit rarely in production.

However, it could be good to be self-consistent. (Otherwise, we could just remove the different error codes and return a single one)

So fix a few error codes:

* An integral out-of-range is now `RPC_TYPE_ERROR`, not `RPC_MISC_ERROR`
* Some invalid args are now `RPC_INVALID_PARAMETER`
* Some transient issues or user-config issues are now `RPC_MISC_ERROR`
* Finally, `RPC_INTERNAL_ERROR` is reserved for internal bugs or internal corruption

pulls.title: refactor : Reorder CBlockIndex members to save 8 bytes
pulls.body:
It seems we can save 8 bytes per CBlockIndex instance by reordering one class member. Moving one 8-byte field seems to avoid losing 2x 4 bytes to structure padding on a 64-bit build (on a 32-bit build, there is no gain).

I could not exactly measure the runtime gain from just this (smaller than RAM usage variation between 2 launches), but I confirmed there was about as many instances of CBlockIndex as blocks in the chain (increasing CBlockIndex size by 320 bytes increases RAM usage by ~300MB), so saving 8 bytes per instance should save about 8MB of RAM at current block height.

The gain is small, but it seems like it has no cost/risk, since that structure is not used for serialization, and just reordering here should have no side effects.

I saw a few other types that could gain a few bytes in size by doing something similar (for example, CTxIn), but they have far fewer instances in memory to make the change worth it.

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization, while becoming very slow to deserialize.

This PR stores the stack as its serialization in a single allocation (or none if the stack is empty), with a small header holding its size and the offset of the last element. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place, only allowing replacing them entirely. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead. `CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes.

Later commits also introduce stricter checking during deserialization, rejecting the following before fully deserializing:
* Transactions with more inputs/outputs than are possible in a valid transaction.
* Transactions with 0 inputs or 0 outputs (applied in P2P, but not RPC etc. for backward compatibility).
* Transactions/blocks that exceed the 4M weight limit (also only applied in P2P).

The result is a significant reduction in the worst-case time and memory allocations needed for deserialization, both in valid and invalid transactions. With it, the worst-case memory of a valid deserialized block drops from 106.8 MiB to 6.0 MiB. Memory usage during deserialization can temporarily be higher: up to 7.8 MiB for valid blocks, and up to 13.4 MiB for invalid blocks, which can combine a few temporary vector allocations of up to 5 MB each.

Deserialization time and memory of the deserialized block, master → PR. Runtimes are medians in milliseconds. Memory usage is in MiB, and ✕ means rejected at deserialization time. Peak memory refers to the memory during deserialization itself, not persisted in the deserialized `CBlock` object. Numbers over 50 ms, 20 MiB usage, or 100 MiB peak are in **bold**.

| block | gcc | clang | mem | peak mem |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Valid blocks** |
| 1 tx, max 1-byte wit elems | **99.1** → 16.0 | **111.4** → 21.9 | **106.8** → 3.8 | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, max empty wit elems | **279.2** → 18.7 | **293.7** → 25.1 | **91.5** → 3.8 | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout, 1-item wit | 12.33 → 13.39 | 15.00 → 15.43 | 6.7 → 6.0 | 6.7 → 6.0 |
| max txs, 1 txin and 1 txout | 6.43 → 7.04 | 7.87 → 8.30 | 5.8 → 5.6 | 5.8 → 5.6 |
| 1 tx, max txins, 1-elem wit | 4.53 → 4.68 | 5.04 → 5.37 | 4.0 → 2.9 | 4.0 → 2.9 |
| mainnet block 969729 | 5.30 → 5.47 | 5.97 → 6.20 | 3.5 → 2.9 | 3.5 → 2.9 |
| **Invalid blocks** |
| 400k txs, many wit elems, truncated | **84.8** → 16.1 | **95.6** → 21.8 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 12.6 |
| 400k txs, big wit+scriptsig, truncated | **84.0** → 16.1 | **96.0** → 21.7 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 13.4 |
| 1 tx, 2M 1-byte wit elems | **98.0** → 10.6 | **109.9** → 16.2 | **106.8** → ✕ | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, 4M empty wit elems | **271.0** → 13.4 | **288.9** → 19.6 | **91.6** → ✕ | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max empty txs | **101.0** → 0.006 | **139.0** → 0.008 | **67.1** → ✕ | 67.1 → 4.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout | 27.6 → 7.3 | 34.5 → 8.5 | **23.4** → ✕ | 23.4 → 6.4 |

So in addition to improving worst cases very significantly, it also provides modest memory usage improvements to the common case. This translates to mildly increasing the effective capacity of memory-bounded data structures that store transactions, like the mempool.

Some notable changes:
* By implementing some checks (for inherently consensus-invalid things) in the deserialization logic, behavior may change. In particular, deserialization errors in P2P cause messages to be dropped/ignored, rather than triggering validation or net processing logic (which may include disconnections and/or inserting into reject filters).
* The rejection of transactions with too many inputs or outputs applies everywhere, including in RPC. That's hopefully a desirable change, but a change in behavior still.
* Random access to the witness stack elements becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$. This is not a problem for any validation logic, but may be relevant for the libbitcoinkernel API which exposes an individual element accessor.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

There are a few possible follow-ups:
* Enforce the 400k WU policy limit during transaction deserialization when active (instead of the 4M WU consensus limit).
* Extend this approach to entire `CTransaction`, allowing all transaction data to be stored packed together in a few allocations (rather than one per input, one per output, one per witness) plus some index structure to access it efficiently. That's a much bigger change, needing abstractions like #35569, but would reduce the maximum memory usage per WU for valid blocks from around 1.5 bytes/WU to 1.1 bytes/WU (compared to ~28 bytes/WU in master).

pulls.title: fuzz: torcontrol: drive the control connection over a mocked socket
pulls.body:
The `torcontrol` fuzz target hands made-up replies straight to the `TorController` callbacks, and caps each reply line at 16 characters. As a result:

- Most success paths can't be reached. They need lines such as `AUTH METHODS=...`, `ServiceID=<v3 id>` or `net/listeners/socks=...`.
- The code that parses bytes from the control port (`ProcessBuffer`, `ReceiveAndProcess`) and the command/reply chain are never fuzzed.

This PR adds:

- Allows reply lines up to 256 characters.
- Builds the values the fuzzer can't produce on its own:
  - v3 onion IDs, which need a checksum;
  - well-formed private keys;
  - `AUTH` lines that point at cookie files created for the test;
  - SAFECOOKIE server hashes.
- Drives a real `TorControlConnection` over a `DynSock`, with the harness playing Tor. This covers split writes, CRLF/LF line endings, async replies, EOF and reconnects. Direct handler calls are kept, so deep paths stay cheap to reach.
- Asserts that every command sent to Tor starts with a known command name and contains no stray line break.
- Keeps the target deterministic:
  - seeds the RNG;
  - clears `mapLocalHost` before each input;
  - only lets `COOKIEFILE` name files the harness created, so Tor input can't make the node read arbitrary host files.

The first commit fixes `DynSock::Wait()`. It wrapped `this` in an owning `shared_ptr`, so the socket deleted itself when the call returned. The bug has been there since #30205 and only showed up once this target called `Wait()`.

Coverage of `src/torcontrol.cpp`:

|        | lines | branches |
|--------|------:|---------:|
| master | 52.2% | 47.5% |
| this PR | 81.8% | 74.0% |

The master numbers come from the current qa-assets corpus. The numbers for this PR come from a short local run starting from the same seeds.

This changes the input format, so the qa-assets corpus for this target needs a refresh. I would be happy to open a a PR on qa-assets with new minimized corpus for this target.

pulls.title: node: batch block file pruning in a single pass over block index
pulls.body:
When starting a node with pruning enabled (e.g. `-prune=550`) on a node with full chain history or pruning many files at once, `FindFilesToPrune` and `FindFilesToPruneManual` previously called `PruneOneBlockFile` once per file.

Because `PruneOneBlockFile` iterated over the entire `m_block_index` for each file, this was an O(M * N) operation (M = files to prune, N = total blocks). When pruning a full chain (~5,770 files and ~972k blocks), this triggered ~5.6 billion iterations and froze the node running on a Pi 5 for ~10 minutes on startup while holding `cs_main`.

This PR replaces `PruneOneBlockFile` with `PruneBlockFiles(const std::set<int>&)`, which collects all candidate files and prunes them in a single O(M + N) pass over `m_block_index` using a compact dynamic bitfield (`std::vector<bool>`). Also skips entries without block or undo data to avoid unneeded checks and prevent file 0 pruning from dirtying header-only or already-pruned index entries. The new signature is analogous to `UnlinkPrunedFiles({file_number});`.

Benchmarked with ~972k blocks and 5,770 files to prune:
- x86_64 (i7-8665U @ 1.90 GHz): 75.1s -> 14.7ms (~5,100x speedup)
- ARM64 (Raspberry Pi 5): 606.0s -> 26.3ms (>3,500x speedup)

Both timings were taken with a datadir whose block index and block file info records came from a full chain, with the `blk*.dat` and `rev*.dat` files backfilled as 0-byte files. Pruning selection reads only the index and the file info, so empty files reproduce the startup cost without a full chain, and `UnlinkPrunedFiles` deletes them cheaply.

A case where this matters in practice is a pruned node restarting after a long outage. It downloads headers for the whole gap first, leaving many header-only entries behind, then has to prune a large backlog in a few flushes. The data-less skip avoids re-dirtying all of those entries, and the single pass bounds the work by the index size instead of files times index size.

Add unit test `blockmanager_prune_block_files_batch` to verify batch pruning, empty set no-ops, clean dirty-set behavior, and cleared block and undo metadata. Add a test for the `FindFilesToPruneManual` caller path, including a mixed valid and out-of-range file set. Update caller tests in `blockmanager_tests` and `rescan_tests`.

Addition, I ran the test on my laptop as well, going from full node to `prune=5000` took 8:11:
```
2026-11-11T16:50:09Z init message: Pruning blockstore…
2026-11-11T16:58:20Z block tree size = 975494
```

pulls.title: validation: throw when a compressed script can't be decompressed
pulls.body:
`ScriptCompression::Unser` ignores the `DecompressScript` return value and
leaves the script empty on failure, without notifying upper layers about the error.
In the worst-case scenario, which is currently only reachable through corruption,
an unspendable off-curve P2PK turns into an anyone-can-spend empty script.
Given that, properly throwing the error to prevent any future mistakes from
happening seems the sanest path to follow.

Aside from that, added coverage for a P2PK script with an uncompressed pubkey
that has a valid X but a wrong Y, which makes it unspendable. Checking we store
such scripts raw and never encode them as 0x04/0x05, as those encodings
serialize X with only Y's parity (not the full Y), which would make decompression
recompute Y from X and turn the unspendable script into a spendable one, which
would not be good.

pulls.title: streams: handle buffered write failures outside the destructor
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Block and undo writers buffer serialized data, then rely on the `BufferedWriter` destructor to write the remaining bytes.
`fwrite()` can report fewer bytes written than requested after a local storage error, e.g., if the filesystem fills up while a block is being written (my 1 TB benchmarking servers have recently been filling up, so I've been seeing these failures more often).
`AutoFile::write_buffer()` converts that result into an exception, and because the destructor is implicitly non-throwing, the exception invokes `std::terminate`.
Calling `flush()` before destruction is insufficient on its own because a failed flush leaves the same bytes pending, so the destructor retries the write while the original exception unwinds.

I introduced this bug in #31551 when adding `BufferedWriter`.

**Fix:** Block and undo writers now flush explicitly before destruction, catch write errors, log their cause, and request normal fatal shutdown, consistently with the adjacent file-close error handling.
`BufferedWriter` clears the pending byte count before writing, preventing a destructor retry after a failed flush.
The destructor uses `Assume` to detect missing explicit flushes before attempting a fallback flush.
`flush()` continues to propagate exceptions, and `AutoFile` remains unchanged.

<details>
<summary>Manual write-error reproducer</summary>

Force the error path in `AutoFile::write_buffer()`:

```sh
sed -i '' '/^.*AutoFile::write_buffer(/,/^}/s/!= src.size()/!= 0/' src/streams.cpp
cmake -B build && cmake --build build -j5 && build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"; echo "exit=$?"
```

Before this change, implicit flushing invokes `std::terminate`:

> libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::__1::ios_base::failure: AutoFile::write_buffer: write failed: unspecified iostream_category error
> zsh: abort      build/bin/bitcoind -regtest -datadir="$(mktemp -d)"
> exit=134

With this change, `bitcoind` logs the write failure, then completes normal shutdown and exits with status 1:

> Checking all blk files are present...
> [error] Failed to write block file FlatFilePos(nFile=0, nPos=8): AutoFile::write_buffer: write failed: unspecified iostream_category error
> ...
> Error: A fatal internal error occurred, see debug.log for details: Failed to write block.
> [error] Writing genesis block to disk failed
> [error] Error initializing block database
> ...
> Shutdown done
> exit=1
</details>

pulls.title: wallet: make migration more robust against failures
pulls.body:
This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

The covered cases are:

1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process. 
Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
 Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention. 
Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.

pulls.title: http: Restore requirement of IPv4 bind success
pulls.body:
### Problem

When bitcoind starts and the HTTP IPv4 listen address is occupied by another process, but the IPv6 address is available, the server fails open and generates a cookie file. When bitcoin-cli runs it picks up the cookie file and sends the credentials in plain text to the non-bitcoind process running on the default IPv4 port. An attacker can then use the credentials to commandeer bitcoind over IPv6.

### Solution

*Safe defaults*:
* When running with default settings, require that the IPv4 bind succeeds.
* When `-rpcbind` is specified, require that all HTTP listen socket binds succeed (fail closed-behavior).

Node operators who only have IPv6 are now required to override `-rpcbind` and `-rpcallowip` to only specify the working interface and allowed subnet if they were not doing so already.

The problem of bitcoin-cli sending the credentials to what could possibly be the wrong process remains **only in non-default setups**.

### History

40b556d3742a1f65d67e2d4c760d0b13fe8be5b7 from 2015 switched the HTTP server from Boost Asio to LibEvent, and binding switched from an attempt at dual-binding IPv4+v6 and falling back to IPv4-only (rpcserver.cpp / `StartRPCThreads()`), to binding IPv4 *or* IPv6 (httpserver.cpp / `HTTPBindAddresses()`). **The current PR restores the prior behavior of IPv4 being mandatory.**

#14968 from 2018 was an attempt to change the behavior to require *all* binds to succeed. But it ran into issues with poor IPv6 support on CI.

### Severity

This credential exfiltration attack requires capability to launch processes on the bitcoind host. If we are on the same account we can already read the cookie credentials off disk. So it's only really interesting when an attacker is on a different user account on the same host.

### Disclaimer

The first and last commits were probably initially generated with the help of silicon LLMs.

pulls.title: Add output script index and corresponding script history RPC
pulls.body:
Add a new index `txoscriptindex` which indexes all output scripts. Introduce a new `getscripthistory` RPC that returns all transactions that create outputs corresponding to the provided scripts, and optionally the transactions that spend those outputs if `txospenderindex` is also configured.

This has been a long-requested feature, attempted in previous PRs (#2802, #3652, #6835, #10370, #14053).
Some concerns raised were about the ability for an index like this to scale. I think the new techniques being used to build the indexes (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35531, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002) alleviate this concern. This index can be synced in a few hours and the current disk usage is ~54 GB. This is less than the ~66 GB `txindex` disk usage in v31 and earlier. This index can also be used with a pruned node, so a full node can be supported in < 100 GB of disk space. Missing blocks are returned by hash and can be requested from peers using `getblockfrompeer`.

Some other previous concerns were more conceptual, that this type of index could encourage address reuse and chain analysis. IMO this ship has sailed, and the current status quo of not shipping an address index is turning off users who expect this functionality. Workarounds involve installing, configuring, and syncing other third-party software, making the UX of using Bitcoin Core in a self-sovereign way unnecessarily difficult.

The index hashes each output script with SHA256, then applies salted SipHash-1-3-UJ and stores a six-byte prefix. This is to support the popular Electrum protocol, which supplies only the script hash. The RPC can also look up by address or descriptors. Ranged descriptors are also supported, so a single RPC call can return the entire history of a receive/change xpub pair.

Because there are some scripts with millions of outputs, we introduce a new `OrderedVarInt` which serializes the block height after the script hash prefix. This lets LevelDB seek directly to the prefix + block height, so we can page by block height range.

To prevent DoS concerns by supplying an address with millions of outputs, the RPC tracks a byte budget of reads and throws immediately if too many reads are attempted. The error message instructs the user to narrow the block range.

Improvements to `txospenderindex` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36480) will also allow us to use that pruned. The end result would allow users to run with all optional indexes (including this one) in < 200 GB of disk space. Of course a larger pruned setting would be desired if many historical block lookups were being requested.

pulls.title: wallet: fix migration with watch-only transactions
pulls.body:
Fixes #36483

As described in the linked issue, migration to descriptor wallets currently fails for legacy wallets that contain no spendable keys and are tracking watch-only transactions.

When a database transaction containing `RemoveTxs()` is aborted, the database rolls back and the registered `on_abort` callback is invoked. The current listener contains an empty `std::function` so calling it throws `std::bad_function_call` and masks the actual migration error.

The first commit changes the callback to a no-op function since no memory cleanup happens on abort. It also adds a unit test to confirm that abort restores the database record and leaves wallet memory unchanged.

After this commit, the [functional test](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36483) supplied by the issue's author reports `Error: Not all transaction records were migrated (-4)`, exposing the migration error previously masked by the abort callback exception.

During wallet migration, `RemoveTxs()` defers deletion of transactions from the original wallet's in-memory `mapWallet` until after the database commit. The current check that requires an empty map before the database commit causes migration  to fail.

The second commit checks that the transaction IDs left in the map exactly match those already scheduled to be removed in the `txids_to_delete` vector. If they match, migration continues and the `on_commit` callback removes those transactions from memory.

A new functional test is added to cover migration of a blank wallet with watch-only transactions. It checks that the destination watch-only wallet retains both transactions and balance, including after unloading and reloading the wallet, without rescanning the blockchain.

pulls.title: guix: backport oscrypto PBKDF2 timing fix
pulls.body:
With substitutes disabled, `guix-codesign` can fail when building [oscrypto](https://pypi.org/project/oscrypto/) 1.3.0. The `test_dump_private` test raises `ZeroDivisionError`.

[Demo] validation: remove AssumeUTXO
pulls.body:
**Draft demo:** this is meant to showcase what complete AssumeUTXO removal could look like and the simplifications that AssumeUTXO currently prevents.
The decision about complete removal is of course still open. This draft is meant to serve as a concrete reference for the smaller proposals below - it's not meant to be merged.

**Smaller PRs:** I will carve out individual changes to gauge interest in each part, and link them here as they are opened.
Some of the findings are useful even if snapshot loading or background validation stays.
Feedback on which parts seem worth pursuing, and in which order, is welcome.

**Motivation:** this follows our in-person discussion at the October 2026 Core Dev meeting.
My impression was that there was rough agreement about the ambiguity background validation introduces: we trust a snapshot enough to use it immediately, but describe that trust as temporary until the same node finishes checking history.

Multiple chainstates affect much more than snapshot loading: ordinary validation changes have to account for different chainstate roles, candidate sets, notifications, downloads, pruning, cache allocation, database lifetimes and locks.
I am not sure this amount of complexity in the most critical part of our codebase is still worth it, given that adoption [isn't where we hoped it would be](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35054#issuecomment-4468360424).
Ordinary IBD is also getting faster: #35295 is already merged, and the upcoming `pruneassumevalid` will make pruned IBD even faster.

Snapshot bootstrapping without background validation can still offer an advantage: a new node becomes usable before ordinary IBD would finish because snapshot loading time scales with the UTXO set size, while ordinary IBD time scales with the blockchain size.
Whether that is worth its maintenance cost is a fair question, and we can discuss it here or in the dedicated PR where I will propose the removal.
Even after removal, we could decide to add it back in a cleaner way, for example isolated through IPC.
This demo makes that cost, and the code we could remove, visible for that discussion.

**Background validation can be considered separately:** if we keep snapshot loading, I would prefer making its trust assumption explicit and distributing verification across ordinary IBD nodes, as proposed in #32377 and #36543.
That could give us wider independent checking of the commitment without making every snapshot user maintain a second chainstate.

Users who want to validate history themselves and transition to an archival node could rebuild with `-reindex` and pruning disabled.
Alternatively, they could run IBD in a separate datadir while their snapshot node remains usable, then switch once it is ready.
@Sjors's #36557 discusses dropping mandatory background sync and these alternatives.

**What the series demonstrates:**

* After the fixture cleanup in #36601, the next eight commits remove background validation while snapshot loading keeps working, a stopping point that can be reviewed on its own.
* The middle commits remove snapshot imports and startup resumption, then the validation, block storage, notification and release-process special cases they needed.
* The final seven commits add the simplifications this removal enables: startup in one pass, stable database ownership, one download path, a single prune height, and removal of the locks and diagnostics used to select and identify chainstates.

Ordinary validation, `-assumevalid`, pruning, `ChainstateManager` and UTXO export (`dumptxoutset`) remain.

**Related work:**

* [AJ's recent faster-loader branch](https://github.com/ajtowns/bitcoin/tree/202610-loadtxoutset-speedy) and [Sjors's chunked-import experiments](https://github.com/Sjors/bitcoin/tree/2026/10/utxo-coin-chunks) explore reducing import overhead while retaining snapshot support.
* #35054 contains the broader discussion about P2P snapshot distribution, its users and its costs.

pulls.title: wallet: check block availability before registering chain notifications in AttachChain
pulls.body:
### Problem
When loading an existing wallet on a node where required blocks are not yet available on disk (for example, on a pruned node or during assumeutxo background sync before historical blocks are downloaded), `CWallet::AttachChain` previously registered `m_chain_notifications_handler` with the chain *before* validating block availability (`rescan_height != block_height`).

When the availability check subsequently failed, `AttachChain` returned `false`, and `CWallet::LoadExisting` disconnected the notifications handler. Calling `DisconnectChainNotifications()` calls `chain().waitForNotifications()`, which drains pending validation interface callbacks. Any `BlockConnected` notifications queued on the scheduler or arriving from background synchronization during that window were delivered to the failing wallet instance. If a delivered block matched wallet transactions or fell on a periodic checkpoint, `CWallet::blockConnected` invoked `WriteBestBlock()`, persisting an updated `CBlockLocator` to disk despite the failed wallet load.

As a result, a wallet that failed to load was mutated on disk with an advanced locator. On the next load attempt after node sync completed, the wallet trusted this corrupted locator and skipped rescanning all preceding blocks, silently missing transactions and reporting incorrect balances (e.g. failing with `AssertionError: not(15.00000000 == 34)` in `wallet_assumeutxo.py`).

Fixes #36828.

### Solution
Perform the block-availability preflight check (verifying `chain.havePruned()` or `chain.hasAssumedValidChain()` against `haveBlockOnDisk`) before registering `m_chain_notifications_handler`. If required historical blocks are missing, `AttachChain` exits immediately with `return false` without ever registering validation callbacks. This ensures that no notifications are queued or delivered to the wallet, preventing any locator corruption or on-disk mutation during a failed load.

### Testing
- Built with CMake 4.3.0 and GCC 16.2.1.
- Unit tests: Verified `test_bitcoin --run_test=wallet_tests,rescan_tests,walletload_tests` (32/32 test cases passed).
- Functional tests: Verified `wallet_assumeutxo.py` passes cleanly (demonstrating that pre-sync failed load does not corrupt the post-sync balance).
- Additional functional regressions: `wallet_basic.py`, `wallet_multiwallet.py`, `wallet_balance.py`, `wallet_backup.py`, `wallet_labels.py`, and `wallet_importdescriptors.py` all passed.

`invalidateblock` returns `null` even when the block was not invalidated because the RPC does not pay attention to `Chainstate::InvalidateBlock()` return value. pulls.title: mining: add getMemoryLoad() and track template non-mempool memory footprint
pulls.body:
IPC clients can hold block templates indefinitely, keeping transactions alive after they leave the mempool. This adds `getMemoryLoad()` to estimate the memory held on behalf of all mining clients, as discussed in bitcoin/bitcoin#33899. It does not impose a limit.

The estimate includes each tracked template's vectors and the transactions it references that are no longer in the mempool. Transaction objects shared by multiple templates are counted once. Dummy coinbase transactions and the template cached by the `getblocktemplate` RPC are excluded.

`BlockTemplateManager` tracks templates through weak references, so the registry does not prolong their lifetime. Templates unregister when destroyed, including when IPC cleanup happens after shutdown has reset the manager. Clients can reduce the reported memory load by releasing stale templates or explicitly calling `destroy()`.

The result is an estimate: the mempool can change during calculation, and eviction followed by re-entry as a different transaction object can cause undercounting.

Example client usage: [stratum-mining/sv2-tp#63](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-tp/pull/63).

Commits:

- `refactor: pass block template by reference to WaitAndCreateNewBlock`
- `refactor: share ownership of BlockTemplateManager`
- `mining: track block templates held by IPC clients`
- `mining: add GetTemplateMemoryUsage()`
- `ipc: add getMemoryLoad()`
- `test: check template memory accounting invariants`

pulls.title: validation: Ensure Invalid ValidationState has result
pulls.body:
Block and transaction validation results are represented in `ValidationState`, and invalid results in "Invalid" states. Invalid validation results have a `result`, an enum value, and a `reject_reason`, a structured string.

The change is to ensure that an __invalid result always has a set result and reject reason__. This increases code robustness/security.

One instance was identified where the result was not set, and is being fixed by a new `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result. PR #31981 moved a previous-block check from outside of `TestBlockValidity()` to inside it, and introduced a new usage of `BlockValidationState` with unset result. The result field is not checked outside. This instance is changed now to use the newly-introduced `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` value.

The new enum value is added to the kernel C API and its C++ wrapper. In P2P, a `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result does not lead to punishing the peer.

A few test-only instances with empty reject reason are changed to use a dummy value ("dummy-reason").

History: this was found on the side of #35570, but left untouched there; see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#issuecomment-5739477357 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#discussion_r4075379069.

pulls.title: p2p: replace full outbound peers that don't support tx relay (take 2)
pulls.body:
Picks up #28538

Outbound-full-relay slots should be used by peers that actually relay transactions, besides #28538 see #16418 and #28371 for the motivation. So try to replace peers that are not relaying txs with peers that do.

The approach differs from the original PR in a few details in response to some of the review comments there:

- A replacement is connected before the peer is evicted. The original PR disconnected a non-tx-relaying peer once all full outbound slots were filled. Reviewers preferred having a replacement available first (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). Now an extra outbound-full-relay connection is requested, like the extra network-specific peers, and the existing eviction of extra outbound peers prefers peers that don't relay txs.
- Peers not relaying txs don't get `m_protect`. Otherwise they could stay forever (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443336121), and ignoring the protection was rejected in the same thread (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443312604).
- An only peer on a network is not replaced. Otherwise the network-specific extra connections and this logic would keep replacing each other (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). This also covers the `-maxconnections=1` case (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1417178196).

Nothing is changed in `-blocksonly` mode or during IBD. The rename commit and the functional test are taken from the original PR with some changes to match the new behavior.

pulls.title: net: serve `MSG_BLOCK` by stripping witnesses in place
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Serving blocks to legacy nodes currently decodes and reserializes them just to remove witnesses. `MSG_WITNESS_BLOCK` already avoids this work by serving the stored bytes directly. Faster witnessless IBD, as proposed in [#36476](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36476), also needs peers to serve these blocks efficiently.

**Fix:** Read disk-backed, non-Signet `MSG_BLOCK` replies into an owned byte buffer, check the header's proof of work and expected hash, and strip witness ranges from that buffer in place.

Extract a shared helper so decoding transactions and skipping their bytes follow the same encoding rules. Signet keeps `ReadBlock` for its solution check. Header checks now precede transaction parsing, so records corrupted in both places can log a different error.

**Performance:**

Time to read a block from disk and build its non-witness message:

| Block | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `block413567` | 1.31 ms | 0.147 ms | **8.9x** |
| Same block with synthetic witnesses | 3.47 ms | 0.374 ms | **9.3x** |

The synthetic fixture adds a 512-byte witness item and an empty item to every input.

**Related work:** This extends the raw witness-block serving added in [#13151](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13151). The [#13011 discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13011#issuecomment-383145046) and the closed [#13098](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13098) identify unnecessary transaction hashing when serving historical blocks. The implementation also builds on the bulk block reads introduced in [#31551](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31551).

pulls.title: [DO NOT MERGE] Erlay: bandwidth-efficient transaction relay protocol (Full implementation)
pulls.body:
Erlay Project Tracking: [#30249](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/30249)
Conceptual Discussion: [#34542](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34542)

---

This is a full implementation of Erlay. Its purpose is to check the integrity and correctness of the implementation against changes/additions that may originate from the review process and/or rebases on top of newer functionality.

This is not to be merged. Functionality will be spread across multiple smaller PRs to ease the review process.

---
## Approach

This approach uses Erlay as a fallback mechanism for transaction propagation. Instead of mixing fanout and reconciliation into a single connection type, the current approach leaves the existing connections as they are, and adds additional low-bandwidth connections to be used in case the node is being eclipsed. This connections should have minimal cost under normal circumstances, and only undergo real traffic in case other 8 full-outbound connections are being captured.

## outbound-full-reconciliation connections

For now, we are adding 4 additional reconciliation-only connections to the node while we test it's impact on real node running the approach. Further analysis may be needed to pick a meaningful value for this. The number of inbound connections should also be scaled based on how many connections we are adding.

pulls.body:
**Problem:** The oversized-script fallback appends `OP_RETURN` to the destination instead of replacing it. If the destination already contains an unfinished push, the appended byte becomes pushed data and the result can remain spendable.

**Fix:** Replace the destination with `OP_RETURN` rather than appending it.

Found while reviewing #36280. This predates that PR and appears latent because oversized outputs are excluded from the UTXO set, but it could affect malformed stored records decoded into a reused destination.

pulls.title: [WIP] wallet: standardize change output detection process
pulls.body:
This work aims to define, and implement a base standard mechanism to
detect individual change outputs.

### Context

Currently, the wallet detects whether an output is change or not based
on data stored in the address book.

There is no notion of “change outputs”, the wallet detects change scripts.

Connoting that any address book record modification has implications
on all the historical outputs related to that particular destination. Meaning
that all those outputs can either be change or not. There is no middle-ground
granular distinction.

#### How Change Detection Currently Works?

The wallet walks-through the transaction outputs, extracts the script
destination and verify the following two points:

1) If the destination doesn't exist in the address book, then the script
    is a "change address".
   
2) If the destination exists in the address book, but it doesn't have a
     label, then the script is a "change address".

### Motivation

There are a good number of problems in the current approach:

- We make the wallet dependent on an external structure, with separate storage.
   Which has to be updated and maintained along with the wallet state.

- It cannot be maintained nor recovered across different wallet instances.
   Cannot re-create the, possibly custom, address book data only by importing
   the wallet descriptor string.

- As the address book is an structure that the user can freely modify, the change
   detection process might differ through different wallets.
 
- The current rudimentary assumptions of "no address book entry" or "no label set for the address book entry"
  to denote that certain script destination is change or not can easily be broken:
  E.g. derive an address from one of the wallet’s external paths manually. Then send coins to it.
  As the receive destination wasn't created inside the wallet, the wallet has no associated address book entry.
  So, the reception is invalidly detected as change (added a test case for it).

- The wallet can't detect change outputs on more complex scripts such as multi-sig change outputs.

- The wallet is not able to detect change outputs going to an internal address if the internal address has a label.
  (E.g. the user can manually set a label for the internal address and, doing that, make that all the change
  outputs, in the wallet history, that were sent to the destination are no longer detected as change).

- There isn’t a way to distinguish the external reception of coins into an internal address. Coins reception on any
   internal address are always detected as change.

### New Change Detection Mechanism Goals

Aiming to:

* Define a base mechanism to align different wallet implementations. Preventing each piece of software
  from diverging on the basic change outputs distinction.

* Detect change outputs on-demand without requiring to maintain an external data structure synced with the
   latest wallet state.

* Independently, and accurately, detect change outputs regardless data stored in structures that the user
   can freely modify.

* Granular distinction between change vs non-change outputs that were sent to the same internal address.
  E.g. the reception of coins, from an external source, on internal addresses will not longer be detected
  as change anymore.

* Expand the change detection to more complex scripts such as a multi-sig protected addresses. (While they
  are added into the wallet on an internal spkm)

#### Change Output Detection Rules

A transaction output is change if it fulfills the following points:

1) At least one of the parent transaction inputs is from the wallet. (If none of them are, then the wallet is receiving coins
    on an internal address).

2) The script extracted destination is from the wallet and is located in one of the internal script pub key manager.
    (e.g. derived from an internal derivation path)

#### What about legacy wallets?

If the legacy wallet is HD post-split, we have an internal derivation path, so we can follow the same process as
descriptors wallet. Unless the destination is on the pre-split key pool, in which case, we fallback to the follow-up
case.

If the legacy wallet is pre-split, we continue using the address book as we either have an HD wallet with keys
derived only on the external path, or we are using raw keypool.

———————————————————————

#### Extra Note
This PR, in about 85% at least, is about expanding the current test coverage for the change output detection area.

#### TO DO (still WIP):

* [x] Save “internal” flag on non-active descriptors so the wallet can use them on the change detection process.
   (which will fix the currently failing test cases).
* [ ] Re-organize commits so tests always pass.
* [ ] Verify backwards compatibility.

pulls.body:
`EventLoop::loop()` exits when its reference count reaches zero. In `serve()` mode, the parent connection is the only reference keeping the loop running. Other `CapnpProtocol` methods called from threads not handling parent IPC requests do not hold their own references and therefore depend on the parent connection remaining alive.

Add `loopRef()` (code suggested by @ryanofsky in https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/376#discussion_r4268952676), which returns a new reference to the event loop or throws if the loop is not running or is shutting down, and use it in the methods that need the loop. Protect `m_loop` with a new `m_loop_mutex` to prevent `serve()` from destroying the loop while `loopRef()` is accessing it.

pulls.title: descriptor: Represent multipath descriptors in a single Descriptor object
pulls.body:
Currently, multipath descriptor strings treat the multipath specifiers as syntactic sugar. Once we finish parsing such a string, the multipath elements are lost as the result is the multiple distinct descriptors that the multipath is a shorthand for. This means that we are unable to return the multipath string for such descriptors.

This PR allows descriptors to actually be multipath where the multipath specifiers are represented inside of the paths of `BIP32PubkeyProvider`s. This allows for the multipath string to be produced.

In order to achieve this, a lot of derivation path parsing is refactored. `KeyPath` is promoted to being its own class (which subclasses `std::vector`), while the individual derivation indexes become a `KeyPathElement` object so that the multipath elements can be represented. Furthermore, hardened derivation characters are now being stored within `KeyPathElement`s so each element knows what the original hardened character was. This also cleans up a little bit of the descriptor implementation as we no longer have to carry around `bool apostrophe` in a bunch of places.

Lastly, `Parse` now returns a single `Descriptor` object, rather than a vector of them. If the descriptor is a multipath descriptor, the expansion can be retrieved using `GetMultipathExpansion()`. The wallet uses this and still must not store multipath descriptors.

pulls.title: http: support unix sockets
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/5029

Accept unix socket paths as options for `-rpcbind=` (server) and `-rpcconnect=` (bitcoin-cli). Options follow the same pattern as `ipcbind`:

- `=unix` is a magic keyword that means `<datadir>/http.sock`
- `=unix:relative/path` means `<datadir>/relative/path`
- `=unix:/absolute/path` means `/absolute/path`

We delete any existing `http.sock` before calling `bind()` and do not clean up at shutdown.

Because access is handled by the filesystem, `-rpcallowip` is ignored for unix sockets and not required at all if we are *only* binding to unix sockets.

Authentication by username/password/cookie is still required.

A new option `--httpunix` is added to the test framework and added to test_runner for `rpc_bind.py` and `interface_http.py` for CI, but (like `--usecli`) most other tests should also pass with that option. When set, bitcoind is started with `-rpcbind=unix...`which overrides `tcp://localhost` entirely. `AuthProxy` has been extended to connect directly to the unix socket.

Try it out!
```
bitcoind -regtest -rpcbind=unix
bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcconnect=unix getbestblockhash
```

Refactored code:

Back in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27375 we added unix socket support but it was isolated to the `Proxy` class. That created a bit of tech debt which we pay off in this PR. Two new classes are implemented:
- `UnixSocketAddr` reflects the `CService` API for generic unix sockets, without bitcoin-p2p-specific attributes
- `SocketAddr` holds a variant of `UnixSocketAddr` and `Cservice` so classes like `Proxy` and `HTTPServer` can operate on an abstract level, with either socket type.
- `CNetAddr` and `CService` are left untouched -- they are somewhat dirty combinations of generic socket classes and bitcoin p2p code, adding unix sockets to those classes wouldn't make sense for bitcoin p2p operations and that's why this design was chosen.

Follow-up suggestions:
- Deduplicate some of the unix socket path resolution code between IPC and HTTP
- On macos the default unix socket buffer size is only ~8k. In the functional tests we have to bump the python client socket buffer up to ~256k or the "throttle" tests will stall on macos. We could apply this socket option on the server side as well, only on macos... requires some bike shedding.
- This option replaces TCP but it does not replace HTTP, there may be a more efficient transport protocol.


Production code and test framework changes designed and authored by my own cranial meatball. Unit tests added by Opus. C++ cleaned up by Fable, security tightened by Kimi-k3 🧠 🤖 🤖 🤖

It knows the transport's keys, builds the input from arbitrary bytes and from parts of a valid handshake (the peer key, garbage, the terminator, encrypted packets that may be corrupted, and runs of empty decoys that force a rekey), and feeds it in pieces of arbitrary size. Once the transport reports v2, it checks that its session id matches the peer's.

It reaches the v2 receive states and their failures, except the fallback to v1 and the wrong-magic disconnect, which need a v1 `version` header at the start of the stream; `p2p_transport_bidirectional_v1v2` reaches the first. 15 minutes with libFuzzer, ASan and UBSan found no crash.

pulls.title: wallet: Store information about created and imported multipath descriptors
pulls.body:
The wallet does not store any information about multipath descriptors. When a multipath descriptor is imported, it is first expanded, then the expansion descriptors are imported into the wallet.

This PR adds a field to `WalletDescriptor` which stores the IDs of the ScriptPubKeyMans of the descriptors that are part of the expansion, in the order that they are expanded. This allows us to use `ReconstructMultipath` to produce the multipath descriptor when necessary.

This is useful for working with hardware wallets that require policy registration, particularly those that require resending the descriptor that was registered.

`listdescriptors` is updated to include a `multipath_descriptor` field which contains the multipath descriptor for each individual descriptor if it originally came from a multipath descriptor.

Lastly, the automatically generated descriptors are now produced and stored as multipath descriptors, so `listdescriptors` will provide a `multipath_descriptor` for everything that the wallet automatically generates.

Note that the IDs stored in the wallet are ScriptPubKeyMan IDs, which we cannot compute from a descriptor as we assume to be opaque blobs since #35445.

pulls.title: rpc: handle malformed jsonrpc 2.0 requests correctly
pulls.body:
While reviewing #36642 I found something else we missed in JSON-RPC 2.0:

If we receive a malformed request we would assume that we couldn't parse it's jsonrpc version and send an HTTP error.  This is how the legacy jsonrpc server worked (despite that behavior not ever being part of any ratified jsonrpc spec) and we maintain it as Bitcoin "legacy" jsonrpc protocol. However it's possible to form a request that does properly indicate jsonrpc 2.0 but is still malformed. In that case, we should not send an HTTP error: the correct protocol is to respond with `HTTP 200 OK` and include the jsonrpc error message in the response.

The solution is to check if we know the request's jsonrpc version before responding with an error.

We already correctly handle such malformed requests in batches and this is already tested in `test_batch_requests()` in `interface_rpc.py`

On master, the functional test in this PR actually crashes the node because the assumption is codified. Note that this crash requires:
1. RPC Authentication
2. A debug build

So this is not an urgent security fix, but a bug that might disrupt testing.

```
node0 stderr httprpc.cpp:46
    UniValue JSONErrorReply(UniValue, const JSONRPCRequest &, HTTPStatusCode &):
        'jreq.m_json_version != JSONRPCVersion::V2' check failed.
```


In release builds the node doesn't crash, but it returns HTTP 400 with a JSON-RPC 2.0 error body instead of HTTP 200.

pulls.title: Implement BIP 54 (Consensus Cleanup) without mainnet activation
pulls.body:
This implements the Consensus Cleanup validation rules proposed in [BIP 54](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0054.md). These rules are only enabled on regtest. Mainnet activation, if any, is to be considered separately.

This patchset is based on the code that was previously reviewed ([1](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/99), [2](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/110)) and tested (for instance [here](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/consensus-cleanup-demo-of-slow-blocks-on-signet/2367)) on Bitcoin Inquisition. pulls.title: rpc: generateblock to allow multiple outputs with custom payouts
pulls.body:
## Generatetomany

First approach was to create a `generatetomany` rpc call. That approach can be seen here https://github.com/polespinasa/bitcoin/pull/3

## Generateblock
Modifies `generateblock` to allow a user to set multiple outputs in the coinbase transaction. If an empty set is provided, the block will be empty. If no set of transactions is provided, the block will mine the mempool. If a set of transactions is provided only that set of txs will be mined.

```
$./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock bcrt1qw6qkj8wtw5hraxwxjp08m4aymkntms3yhqyacj
{
  "hash": "7359a3ed7af0f18f4016e6cb29193bd787a2452c584781135c585d5204b9ec5b"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]'
{
  "hash": "6db028454b26d6667dd6df45be2772844121fb44f86433f6bbfbafa429974684"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]' []

{
  "hash": "33e2ddc52546ddb0edf28bef5b295ee8fbd487b8aca19c97018467e2477877df"
}

```

### Motivation
https://x.com/SuperTestnet/status/1921220086645342550

Citating @supertestnet 
> When mining a block on regtest, the command "generatetoaddress" is available if you want to send the entire coinbase to 1 address. Let's add generatetomany in case you want to split up the coinbase among multiple addresses, similar to how the "sendtoaddress" and "sendmany" commands both exist and let you send money to (1) one address or (2) multiple addresses. The generatetomany command would be particularly useful for simulating protocols that send money to multiple recipients directly from a coinbase, as several pools do now, like ocean and braidpool.

pulls.title: test: Add test coverage for `PartiallySignedTransaction::Merge()`
net: prevent duplication manual connections (take 2)
pulls.body:
Fixes #5299.

`-connect` and `-addnode` can attempt the same manual connection concurrently during startup. The existing duplicate checks cannot see a peer until it has been added to `m_nodes`, so both attempts can pass and open connections.

Reserve the destination in `OpenNetworkConnection()` before checking connected peers or starting the connection. The reservation stays in place until the attempt fails or the new peer has been added to `m_nodes`.

This applies to `ConnectionType::MANUAL`, including `-connect`, `-addnode`, manual reconnections, and `addnode onetry`. Automatic outbound connections are outside this change.

The functional test checks the original two-node startup case. It also holds a manual connection in a local proxy handshake and verifies that an overlapping attempt is rejected, that a failed attempt releases its reservation, and that equivalent numeric addresses share a reservation.

Unlike #27804, this handles attempts in the connection manager rather than deduplicating configuration arguments. Hostnames use their original string as the reservation key, so different names that resolve to the same endpoint may still overlap. This avoids an extra DNS lookup.

pulls.title: rpc: Report -rpcwhitelist denials as JSON-RPC errors
pulls.body:
This PR adds two JSON-RPC error codes for requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist`, which until now got an HTTP 403 status with an empty body:

- `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` (-38) is returned for a refused request, with HTTP 200 for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and 403 for legacy 1.x requests.
- `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` (-39) is returned for the other requests in a refused batch. A refused batch now gets HTTP 200 and an array with an error for each request, and still runs none of them.

**Problem:** `-rpcwhitelist` errors are currently handled differently from other JSON-RPC errors, so clients report them with vague or misleading messages, and for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests the handling does not follow [documented behavior](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/doc/JSON-RPC-interface.md#json-rpc-11-vs-20). Specifically, requests refused by `-rpcwhitelist` get HTTP 403 with an empty body, so the refusal shows up as a generic transport error rather than a specific JSON-RPC error. This is especially a problem for JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, which are [supposed to](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/bf1a1f1662427fbf1a43bb951364eface469bdb7) report failed method calls only as JSON-RPC errors, not HTTP errors. The empty reply causes a concrete problem when JSON-RPC requests are sent over IPC instead of HTTP: `bitcoin-cli -ipcconnect` receives only the response body, so a refused call prints a JSON type error instead of a permission error, as described in a [private security review](https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/audits/ar-56/). Over HTTP, `bitcoin-cli` currently stops at the 403 status and prints only "server returned HTTP error 403" instead of the actual error.

**Solution:** Report whitelist denials like any other failed call: a JSON-RPC error in the body, with the HTTP status the request's version calls for. This brings the behavior in line with the documentation. `bitcoin-cli` then prints the permission error over both HTTP and IPC, with no change to the IPC interface. Small change to `src/httprpc.cpp` and `src/rpc/protocol.h`, with tests in `rpc_whitelist.py` and `interface_ipc_cli.py`. Details in the commit messages.

Compatibility: HTTP clients that send `"jsonrpc": "2.0"` or batches and check for a 403 status need to read the error code instead. Single 1.x requests keep the 403 status, now with an error body.

Open question for review: `RPC_METHOD_NOT_PERMITTED` could be named `RPC_ACCESS_DENIED`, and `RPC_REQUEST_NOT_EXECUTED` is documented as batch-specific but would fit any request refused before it runs.

pulls.title: wallet: harden external signer psbt processing, revamp mock
pulls.body:
The current external signer functional test mock can only echo a prepared PSBT. This gets in the way of testing more complicated scenarios, i.e. misbehaving signers and (MuSig2) multisig.

- *test: have external signer mock use a wallet*: gives the mock its own offline node and wallet with private keys, while the test uses the watch-only version.
- *external_signer: require matching PSBT versions*
- *external_signer: merge PSBT response instead of replacing*: tests signers that drop outputs, reduce their value or change the script. Merging rejects these changes while allowing signers to omit unnecessary PSBT fields.
- *external_signer: reject unsafe sighash types*
- *external_signer: **reject finalized PSBT inputs***: keeps the above check simple. Documents this new requirement. HWI does not finalize.

The remaining commits prepare the test helpers and enforce IWYU for `src/external_signer.cpp`.

This PR absorbs the scenarios from #35358, but is better able to test them thanks to the new mock signer implementation.

This PR does not intend to fully harden against a malicious external signer, and can't protect against a malicious HWI (equivalent) process running as the same user.

pulls.title: test: allow 3 bytes of fee overestimate in assert_fee_amount
pulls.body:
The wallet sizes a transaction assuming a 71-byte low-R ECDSA signature. A signature whose r or s has leading zero bytes is shorter, so the fee can cover a few bytes more than the signed transaction needs. In #36394 the wallet estimated 219 bytes and paid 438 sat at 2 sat/vB, but the signed transaction was 216 bytes: the signature was 3 bytes short. That happens about once in 4 million signatures. `assert_fee_amount` allows only 2 bytes of overestimate, so the test failed.

I raise the allowance to 3 bytes, which makes the failure about 200 times rarer. The check that the fee is not too low is unchanged. @maflcko suggested 3 bytes in #24151 and #25164.

Fixes #36394.

*Made with my usual tools: a computer, the Internet and an LLM. The mistakes, as usual, are all mine.*

pulls.title: [wip,nomerge,rfc] build: Require C++23 compiler
pulls.body:
C++23 for Bitcoin Core is mostly a "style update" on top of C++20. However, the workarounds to avoid C++23 keep accumulating and some parts of the code already use C++23 features, such as lambda attributes (https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/commit/bdd0cd69418d189f62699d274a751cbf6d36bb43).

I don't know when it is fine to switch, but at some point, I think it is fine to require a C++23 compiler, so that [new stuff](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34979#issuecomment-4448399166) is unlocked. Of course this requires bumping the minimum required compiler versions:

* GCC: 13
* Clang: 19

There are some C++23 features that aren't implemented (such as `<stacktrace>` not really shipped in any vanilla stdlib today), or e.g. `ranges::starts_with` not implemented until libstdc++-16. But overall I think we are better off using C++23 without those few features instead of waiting longer?

pulls.title: depends: fix non-atomic reads in capnp debug assertions
pulls.body:
KJ's debug assertions read the mutex futex word and `AtomicRefcounted` refcounts non-atomically. The TSan job builds capnp without optimization, which automatically enables these assertions, and TSan reports these reads as data races the moment KJ objects start communicating across threads.

libmultiprocess enables cross-thread communication for the first time in bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#376, which replaces the pipe used in `EventLoop::sync()` with `kj::Executor::executeSync()`. This is what triggered the [failure](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/actions/runs/38094008438/job/114336046070?pr=376).

Patches are the upstream commits capnproto/capnproto@b91a6ba7c7 and capnproto/capnproto@cc13c8c45f, which are backports of the v2 fixes in capnproto/capnproto#2781 and capnproto/capnproto#2843 (backport PR: capnproto/capnproto#2855).

pulls.title: wallet: Only broadcast resubmitted transactions that were added to the mempool
pulls.body:
As discussed in #36403, one of the issues with current rebroadcast behavior is that the rebroadcast begins an unconditional relay of a transaction to peers. While this is broadcast is limited to peers that have not previously been inv'd the transaction, there is still a privacy leak in this double relay of a transaction, especially so for transactions that are still in nodes' mempools.

This PR changes the rebroadcast to only rebroadcast transactions if the transaction was not already present in our mempool. This provides some additional privacy while retaining intended rebroadcast behavior as transactions that have likely fallen out of nodes' mempools are the ones that actually need to be rebroadcast.

The wallet rebroadcast tests are additionally refactored for isolation so that their behaviors can still be tested after this change. Additionally, a test for the loading resubmission was added, as well as a test for the new behavior.

pulls.body:
In `doc/i2p.md`, the Compatibility section stated that any SAM v3.1 router can be used.
Bitcoin Core now relies on a feature that requires recent routers:

- `i2cp.leaseSetEncType=6,4` (introduced in #35696)

This is supported by Java I2P ≥ 2.10.0 and i2pd ≥ 2.58.0.

This pull updates the routers list with those minimum versions and adjusts the Compatibility section.

pulls.title: i2p: pass base32 address directly to stream connect
pulls.body:
As the SAM protocol accepts a `.b32.i2p` address as the `DESTINATION` parameter for the `STREAM CONNECT` command, the `NAMING LOOKUP` round trip can be skipped on every outbound connection.

This should ostensibly make failure handling more accurate in certain situations as well, since a peer that cannot be resolved now returns `CANT_REACH_PEER`/`TIMEOUT` rather than there being an empty `VALUE=` key in the lookup reply. A missing `VALUE=` is a proxy error, so the attempt isn't recorded in AddrMan.

Router implementation versions that support this (Java I2P 0.9.48, i2pd 2.38.0) are older than ones supporting `i2cp.leaseSetEncType=6,4` (see #35696), so there should be no compatibility issues here.

Source:
https://i2p.net/en/docs/api/samv3/#sam-virtual-streams-connect

pulls.title: interfaces: Avoid node crashes from invalid Chain IPC calls
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A program using the `Chain` IPC interface from #29409 can crash `bitcoin-node` with a single bad call: asking for a block hash above the tip, passing a negative height to `hasBlocks`, leaving the transaction argument of `broadcastTransaction` or `checkChainLimits` unset, or returning an error from a notification handler. Separately, `findAncestorByHash` reports success when the descendant block is unknown (#36472). The `Chain` methods were written for in-process C++ callers like the wallet, which follow documented preconditions, so they assert or dereference null instead of returning errors.

**Solution:** Make these `Chain` methods in `src/node/interfaces.cpp` return errors for invalid arguments, catch and log IPC errors from notification handlers, and fix the `findAncestorByHash` check. Three small commits, each with unit tests in `src/test/interfaces_tests.cpp`. Valid calls behave the same as before. Details are in the commit messages.

This PR does not depend on #29409, but the fixes matter if it is merged and `interfaces::Chain` is exposed over IPC. The problems were reported by zaidmstrr, willcl-ark and xyzconstant while reviewing #29409, by enirox001 in #36472, and by cyb3ralbert and xyzconstant here (`hasBlocks`). The `findAncestorByHash` fix is the same one previously proposed by Romansage6 and Yudis-bit in #36473, #36484 and #36490.

Fixes #36472.

mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pulls.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.

pulls.title: Enclose all header content in include guards
pulls.body:
From https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/cpp/Once-Only-Headers.html:
> If a header file happens to be included twice, the compiler will process its contents twice. This is very likely to cause an error, e.g. when the compiler sees the same structure definition twice. Even if it does not, it will certainly waste time.

This PR fixes the three headers that have content outside their guards and modifies [`test/lint/lint-include-guards.py`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/test/lint/lint-include-guards.py) to catch such violations in the future.

A prerequisite for https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36808.

pulls.title: contrib: ci: Monitor Windows signing certificate expiry
pulls.body:
Currently we have no automation in place to check that our code signing certificates are not expired or close to expiry. We have previously "relied on Release Candidates" as a dry-run for codesigners to realise that a certificate has expired and have time to fix it. "Noticing during RC cycle" also might not be appropriate in the future if we release more bugfix minor/patch releases on short notice.

In place of this process we can run a weekly CI job which will check the certificate's validity and open an issue when it passes an expiry threshold.

In this draft we only check the windows cert (as I couldn't find a mac one) and we set the alert threshold to 90 days.

When the threshold is passed, the job will open an issue in this repo (optionally tagging relevant key-holders).
